contentBlocks.text: Have you ever noticed a puppy looks like a dog, not a cat? Today we start a new unit exploring why young animals look like their parents.

Young animals generally resemble their parents — a kitten grows features similar to its cat parents, a duckling grows up looking like its duck parents, and a calf grows up looking like its cow parents. This pattern — offspring resembling their parents — happens across almost all animals. Name one animal parent and its young, and describe one way they look similar.
You just identified a real pattern: young animals resemble their parents. Tomorrow we'll see this same pattern in plants!

objectives: Describe the general pattern that young animals resemble their parents
Identify one specific animal-parent/offspring pair and a shared trait
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the new unit and the puppy/dog example.
2. Discuss 2-3 more animal-parent/offspring pairs together (kitten/cat, duckling/duck, calf/cow).
3. Have the child name one pair and describe a shared trait.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Close by looking at a real photo of an animal family, if available.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just one very familiar animal pair (like puppy/dog) rather than covering several
Ready for more: ask the child to think of an animal pair where the young one looks quite different at first (like a tadpole/frog) and discuss why
This is the first lesson of a new unit — a good moment to frame the whole week's exploration of parent-offspring resemblance
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a discussion and drawing activity — check that the child can name a real animal-parent/offspring pair and describe at least one shared trait.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 1 standard 1-LS3-1: young animals resembling their parents, the foundational pattern this new unit explores across animals and plants.
